entries.title: The Generational Difference in Southern Manners
entries.summary: For centuries, some have lamented the erosion of the region’s distinctive approach to etiquette.
entries.content:
For centuries, some have lamented the erosion of the region’s distinctive approach to etiquette.

This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.

It is a truth universally acknowledged that the southerner is the most mannerly person in America. Before any Yanks get defensive, I want to clarify that this does not necessarily make them the kindest group in America. As a young child in Tennessee, I learned that a “Bless your heart” to one’s face paired particularly well with a cutting remark behind closed doors. I also learned that etiquette was a pesky but persistent thing: Anytime I replied to my father with a curt “yes,” he’d look at me sideways and say, “Yes, what?” I’d sigh. “Yes sir.”

My father is a seventh-generation Kentuckian, and my mother’s family has lived in the South since the 18th century. Growing up, I knew that there was a regalia to the southerner’s manners that might come as a surprise to those who cast the region as unrefined. Men are to hold doors for their dates and give up their seats to women on the bus. In some spaces, they will still stand when a lady enters or exits the room. There are also the more casual types of  manners. When you pass any stranger on the street, you say, “Howdy,” or, “How are you?” You wave at pedestrians you drive by in your truck. You let neighbors borrow an egg or a cup of sugar without any expectation of repayment. Even as the identity of the South evolves, and more young people lose certain traits that are identifiably southern, manners remain one of the region’s most distinctive and steadfast qualities.

The region’s attitudes toward hospitality are a natural outgrowth of these broader social graces. In the South, people like to emphasize that anyone’s cousin’s neighbor’s friend will be welcome in your home. As Walter H. Page described in The Atlantic in 1881, if a stranger comes “with a letter of introduction from some of their old friends, or if he happen to be connected, however distantly, with an old family known to them, he will at once be taken into their homes, and he will receive every hospitality.” This kindness has its limits, however. “The South is famous for its courtesy, but the highly refined concept of honor that largely produced its manners has also helped to make the region the most violent in the country,” Benjamin Schwarz noted in a 1997 Atlantic essay. “As the old saying goes, a southerner is gracious and friendly until he is mad enough to kill you.”

Although plenty of southerners are motivated to adhere to codes of etiquette by a sense of selflessness and responsibility, the manners that they are so careful to keep are also an effort to protect their reputation. And a well-mannered person isn’t necessarily a mild-mannered person. One 1996 study compared the behaviors of white male University of Michigan students who grew up in the North with those who grew up in the South: When a man bumped into a student and called him an asshole, the students raised in the South were more likely to think that their masculine reputation was threatened and respond aggressively.

You also cannot tell the story of southern manners without telling the story of Black southerners—specifically, the story of their enslavement and its lingering effects. “A Southerner of the upper class delighted in saying that he was taught his manners by his ‘Black Mammy,’” Jessie W. Parkhurst, the then-dean of women at the Tuskegee Institute, wrote in 1938. Many enslaved women who worked domestic roles were made to care for white children. Beginning in the antebellum era, they were caricatured as grateful and devoted caregivers, even as they were being underpaid and overworked. Long after the abolition of slavery, many white southerners, including my father, who was born into the first breaths of the civil-rights movement, were still raised by Black nannies. (This is true outside the South as well—the majority of domestic workers in America today are women of color.) My father, like many other white southerners, learned most of his manners from the nanny with whom he spent so many hours of his childhood.

The courtesies shown in the region have long been “the product of the fusion of black and white attitudes,” Schwarz noted in his essay. But politeness was often forced on Black southerners because their lives depended on it: As recently as decades ago, any perceived violations of etiquette, including simply making eye contact with white people, could provoke brutal beatings and lynchings. And Black contributions to manners were rarely given equal import. After slavery was outlawed, Black women had limited employment prospects in the Jim Crow era and the years after, and they were usually severely underpaid.

Today, the extent to which southerners are mannerly has evolved, as all things do. Some southerners lament what they see as a recent loss to their distinctive approach to etiquette, but this was already the case in 1897, when W. P. Trent wrote in this magazine, “We have seen that the Southerner’s basis of character is a fine one, and that he is becoming, year by year, more thoroughly nationalized.” He explained that “external manners have undoubtedly changed: there is now less suavity, less punctiliousness, less attention to small details, than of old; but this was true of the South of 1860 as compared with that of 1760, and means nothing but progress in the direction of greater freedom and individuality in conformity with the rest of the world.”

Part of the reason could be that more people are moving to the South. In January, I wrote about the disappearing southern drawl, another aspect of the region’s culture that is noticeably changing. I noted that, according to the U.S. census, the South gained more residents than all other regions combined from 2023 to 2024. I also found that the proliferation of the internet has undeniably altered southern culture; young kids are exposed to different behaviors on social media, and their role models aren’t just nannies or teachers or parents—they now come in the form of content creators and online friends.

These factors may be driving the shift in southern manners writ large. I’ve observed a generational difference even in my own family. My sisters still live in Tennessee, and I live in New York City, but none of us spends our days quite like our mother. She will make warm conversation with strangers whenever she possibly can. Living in a big city can often hurry me out of this habit. She’ll fill your plate a second or third time despite your saying you couldn’t possibly have another bite. I offer my guests a glass of wine and whatever nonperishable snack they can scavenge from the pantry. She will listen to a story she has heard hundreds of times with the enthusiasm of it being its first telling.

My sisters and I don’t have this same patience. But time spent with my mother, who puts hours of care and kindness into daily interactions, always reminds me of the goodness to be found in doing the mannerly thing—in being inquisitive, leaving a kind note, shouting “How are ya?” at the neighbor, knowing that it may turn into a two-hour conversation. Sometimes these niceties are more than just nice. In an age of constant hurry, they’re also an excuse to slow down, if only for a moment.

entries.title: The Wrath of MAGA
entries.summary: The ferocity of the response to Jon Ossoff reveals something deeper about the world of Trump supporters.
entries.content:
The ferocity of the response to Jon Ossoff reveals something deeper about the world of Trump supporters.

MAGA world is angry. Again.



The target this time is Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator from Georgia. At a reelection rally in Atlanta on August 16, Ossoff was attacking President Trump over the Iran war when he pivoted to a more personal attack on the commander in chief. “The president sleeps through his meetings,” Ossoff said. “He golfs and trades stocks. See, he doesn’t want to do the job. He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar.”



Those three words—travel with Natalie—sent MAGA world into paroxysms of rage that have yet to subside.



Natalie is a reference to Natalie Harp, the president’s 35-year-old special assistant, who is known as “the human printer” because she accompanies the president carrying a portable printer and battery pack. She uses it to print out hard copies of positive news articles, flattering social-media posts, and polling data to hand-deliver to him on the go.

What Trump’s defenders heard in Ossoff’s line was innuendo. The White House tore into Ossoff. The White House aide Stephen Miller said the senator’s comments are “among the most vile things I’ve seen in American politics.” White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said Ossoff is “a miserable person who hates this country.” He also referred to Ossoff as “Jon Jerkoff” and as “the biggest cuck loser in politics.” The White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to him as a “cringeworthy feminine theater kid” and a “lightweight loser.” When the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes asked about Ossoff’s comments, the White House Official Rapid Response X account responded by saying, “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.” The president, for his part, referred to Ossoff as a “Pee-wee Herman look-alike.” The MAGA ecosystem—podcast hosts, radio-talk-show hosts, political commentators, and others—followed suit. The Rage Machine was in full operation.

What are we to make of the ferocity of the response? The first thing to note is how over-the-top it was, even by MAGA standards. In a pre-Trump world, Ossoff's comments would have been considered edgy. Today they seem almost restrained, even quaint. The president himself, in the early hours of most mornings, posts things about his critics that are meaner and more insulting by orders of magnitude, and no one in his orbit blinks. They tolerate it and, in many cases, delight in it.

The response was also not smart politics. As my colleague Jonathan Lemire wrote, it served only to draw more attention to the story. By elevating the remark, the White House and Trump’s supporters turned a rally line into a week of national coverage, reinforcing the impression of a presidency defined by dysfunction and insularity. Ossoff, an effective Trump critic, got a much larger national audience for free.

So why did MAGA world respond as it did? One explanation is psychological. In 2016, Trump found a constituency already primed for grievance, and taught it to want more. His supporters have kept themselves in a state of frenzy ever since. They need to be perpetually outraged, aggrieved, and insulted. MAGA world has become addicted to the feeling. It delivers a jolt of adrenaline, it provides a feeling of social belonging, and it gives people a sharpened sense of purpose. They see themselves as warriors in a drama of their own construction. They view their opponents—Democrats, progressives, critics of Trump—as personifications of evil. Inflicting pain on their enemies feels good, really good, and it feels just.

Trump is aware of all of this. It’s why, during the 2024 campaign, he spoke directly to his supporters, saying, “I am your warrior. I am your justice. And for those who have been wronged and betrayed: I am your retribution.”

The attacks on Ossoff are also a response to Trump’s collapsing support and the fracturing MAGA movement. Trump’s supporters need to find a common enemy. The Ossoff comments have given them a chance to lash out, to go on the offensive, and to shake feelings of powerlessness and impending doom. At a time when defending Trump is nearly impossible, attacking his opponents becomes imperative.

But there’s something else going on as well, at least with one subgroup of Trump supporters. I have in mind people who are not true believers but who, for a variety of reasons, long ago made their peace with Trump. These are people—many radio and television commentators, podcasters, and members of Congress among them—who were dedicated conservatives before Trump came along. They believed character was destiny and virtue mattered; they revered the rule of law, institutions, and norms; they championed free trade and free markets, fiscal responsibility, and a strong Western alliance; and they opposed patrimonialism, corruption, and lawlessness in the presidency.

They have given up on all of those commitments, and so much more, as the cost of supporting Trump. The cost of speaking out against him, even when they knew better, was simply too high. They wanted to stay in the good graces of those in power. So they broke. And they know they broke.

This has caused a painful degree of cognitive dissonance within many of them. They want to think better of themselves—and others to think better of them—than their actions warrant. What they see in Ossoff’s comments is a chance to signal that they are still who they once were, or at least seemed to be. In this case, they are portraying themselves as enraged at Ossoff’s “misogynistic lies.” His comments are “repulsive” and “guttersnipe statements.” The senator from Georgia is a “disgusting coward” and a “disgusting pig.” We’re told, “You don’t get lower than that.” They are offended that Ossoff is “punching down” at “defenseless” women.

One can almost hear, from the distant past, their words of moral outrage at Bill Clinton for his affair with Monica Lewinsky. Of course, in this case, Trump supporters have aligned themselves with a man who was found liable for sexually abusing and defaming a woman. Who falsified business records to conceal a sex scandal with a porn star shortly after the birth of his child. Who celebrated his affairs through tabloids. Who said if you have power, you can “grab ’em by the pussy.” Who has called women “fat pigs” and “piggy,” “slobs” and “disgusting animals,” and “horseface.” Who suggested that tough questioning by a woman was due to menstruation. And who has said that “it doesn’t really matter” what the media write “as long as you’ve got a young and beautiful piece of ass.”

But no matter. For these gallant souls, for these defenders of women and their honor, the words that crossed the line of decency were travels with Natalie.

The president’s relationship with Natalie Harp is troubling, but not because there’s any evidence of inappropriate behavior between the 80-year-old Trump and his young aide, a graduate of Liberty University and the product of a deeply conservative evangelical subculture. What there is evidence of is something that, from the perspective of the nation, is quite worrisome: the president’s senescence, and how it manifests itself.

Harp’s path to Trump world began when she said Trump literally saved her life because he approved clinical trials that cured her bone cancer. Experts cast doubt on the story, but it served as her launchpad into Trump world. She is now among his closest aides, almost always by his side.



We know, too, from the letters Harp has sent to Trump that she is obsessed with him. She views him reverentially. According to reports, Harp is with Trump almost around the clock without ever taking a day off. In one letter she wrote, “I want things to always be right between us. I also know I’ve been distracted all week (forgetting to eat throughout the days, and even forgetting to sleep, and only catching a couple hours at a time).”

She has described the president as her “Guardian and Protector in this Life.” She has said to him, “You are all that matters to me” and “I never want to bring you anything but joy.” She has described herself as “unworthy” of him and signed letters to him, “With all my heart, Natalie.” At the close of another letter, she quoted Jane Austen: “I could not have parted with you, to anyone less worthy.”

I have worked in the White House and three administrations. Trust me when I say this is not normal. It’s little wonder that, prior to Trump’s second term, the Secret Service was reportedly alarmed by some of Harp’s letters.

For his part, Trump has become emotionally reliant on her. In Regime Change, the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported that Trump believes she is the only person who loves him as much as his family does. He’s told his staff, “All of you will go off and make money. She’ll never leave me.” In July, when Trump left Turkey on an unmarked plane after reports of an Iranian assassination threat, Trump took only a handful of people on the flight with him. Harp was one of them.

Their relationship appears enmeshed and pathological. And from this distance, based on what I can piece together, she strikes me as a young person, perhaps wounded by life, and desperately in search of something she thinks she will find in this president. That she won’t will ultimately only make things worse for her. The concern for all of us, though, is what she’s enabling.

Harp is “a one-woman conduit of information operating entirely outside the usual chain of command,” as the Times describes her. The information she passes along to him is unvetted, unfiltered, and highly warped and unreliable. She is a pipeline from the MAGA ecosystem to the president. (She reportedly supplied him with the video he posted depicting the Obamas as apes.) She is further distorting the world for a man who, with every passing year, is detaching more and more from reality. His world is narrowing to a pinhole.

That’s never a good thing, but when it happens to the man heading the most powerful country in history, with the most formidable fighting force ever assembled, it could be catastrophic. Late in the life of Donald Trump, the worst qualities of the man, never a secret, are emerging as never before.

Gabriel García Márquez’s novel The Autumn of the Patriarch is about an unnamed dictator, an illiterate who rises to power and brutally takes control of a country. We’re told about “the perfidy within the presidential palace itself” and of “the greed within the adulation and the wily servility among those who flourished under the umbrella of power.”



The “autumn” in the title refers to the corrupt patriarch’s physical and mental decay, his growing paranoia, his psychological isolation, and his inability to form genuine human connections. He surrounds himself with sycophants, creating a false reality, complete with fake news and newspapers, including a single copy of the national daily newspaper—the news rewritten to please him, created only for the dictator. He needs it to maintain his “throne of illusions.”

Ultimately, we know, thrones of illusion do collapse—and not only in novels.

entries.title: The Supreme Court Isn’t Interested in Facts
entries.summary: In decision after decision, the conservative justices are ignoring the evidentiary record that lower courts have worked hard to establish.
entries.content:
In decision after decision, the conservative justices are ignoring the evidentiary record that lower courts have worked hard to establish.

The Roberts Court is abdicating one of its most important roles, that of truth-teller.

This much was apparent on Monday in Trump v. California, when the Supreme Court’s Republican appointees let the Trump administration move forward with a plan to curb voting by mail. Via the Court’s shadow docket, the justices lifted an injunction against parts of an executive order that President Trump had issued to stop what he believes is the “massive cheating that’s gone on” in American elections, as he said at the Oval Office signing ceremony in March.

The Court’s order is troubling on many axes. It injects needless chaos into the midterm elections that are a little more than two months away, restoring, at least formally, one of the administration’s chosen tools for hampering a method that millions of Americans use to vote. It emboldens those already gunning for a more wholesale attack on democratic institutions, a base enthralled by the president’s election lies and White House officials’ willingness to use the machinery of the federal government to preserve their power.

The ruling is also troubling for what it says about the Court and its relationship to facts. Confronted with an imagined crisis of rampant voter fraud, the Court constructed an illusion of its own. It reimagined what the executive order did and glossed over the intentions of the man who signed it. This willingness to both ignore facts and conjure fantasies is not a one-off.

The mail-in-ballots case grew out of a conspiracy theory that Trump has long promoted: American elections are riddled with fraud on a grand scale, and voting by mail is a chief conduit. The March executive order was intended to target this supposed problem. Twenty-three states (along with the District of Columbia) sued, taking issue with three parts of the order.

The first directed federal agencies to compile “state citizenship lists,” presumably as a precursor to purging voter-registration rolls. The second instructed the Postal Service to restrict delivery of mail-in ballots based on these makeshift lists. The third threatened prosecution of state officials who provided ballots to voters deemed ineligible.

The states’ lawsuit objected on both constitutional principle—especially the Constitution’s assignment of election administration to the states—and pragmatic grounds about the burdens of compliance with a muddled order that creates real problems by chasing phantom ones.

In late June, Judge Indira Talwani of the Federal District Court in Massachusetts agreed with them and issued a narrow, temporary block on parts of the order. Her opinion was not some dashed-off expression of her particular preferences. Rather, she undertook a granular evidentiary analysis—the trial court’s métier—scrutinizing how the order had already diverted election officials’ work assignments in Connecticut, affected ballot designs in Massachusetts, and collided with an approaching voter-registration deadline in New Mexico. A federal appeals court endorsed her factual analysis and declined to overturn her order.

The Trump administration then sought emergency intervention from the Supreme Court, which the conservative justices obliged this week. And yesterday, Judge Talwani lifted her injunction, saying the majority’s emergency opinion tied her hands.

Yet the majority’s opinion pays no mind to the undisputed facts. It contains nothing about what Judge Talwani probed, nothing about the burdens it found resulted from the executive order, nothing about a president with delusions of widespread fraud and ambitions of authoritarianism. Instead, the Court inhabits the antiseptic register of institutional injury, abstracting Trump into an ordinary president pursuing reasonable policies “regarding election integrity” and rendering the district court an overzealous judge frustrating the president’s good-faith-policy “goals” with a “string of speculations.”

The damage from the decision occurs at several levels. It includes the slow unraveling of constitutional structure when a rogue executive encroaches on territory assigned to others, in this case Congress and the states; the institutional signaling when the Court blesses that encroachment; the deepening tangle of the Court’s election-law jurisprudence, incoherent as doctrine but reliable in outcome, with the Republican appointees’ delivering on Republican interests; the diminishing of public trust in the Court; and the shunting of impositions and uncertainties onto the people who run elections and the people who vote in them.

For the states, these impositions and uncertainties are not theoretical. As Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote in her dissent, the record and the district court established that Trump’s order had already placed an “incredible strain” on officials who must now spend time and money to “coordinate the implementation of the changes” created by the order on “compressed timelines” and with “limited resources” in a tense political climate.

Jackson launched a subtler and seemingly technical objection in a footnote. The strains on the states, she stressed, “by the way, are facts” found by a district court. Her italicized reference called attention to facts as they operate in law, and to the entitlement of such findings to “clear-error deference,” a procedural rule that bars a reviewing court from setting aside facts found by a lower court unless they are “clearly erroneous,” not merely contestable.

But the Court under Chief Justice John Roberts has made a practice of doing just that, evading facts found by district courts to facilitate ideological objectives, something I describe in a forthcoming article in the Michigan Law Review. This approach predates Trump 2.0, but it has been particularly pronounced in the second term, especially in shadow-docket orders reinstating his policies. We saw it last fall in Noem v. Vasquez Perdomo, in which a district court had documented the terrors and indignities of the immigration raids that the administration inflicted on Latino residents of Los Angeles. On the shadow docket, the Court’s Republican appointees green-lighted the raids, and Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a concurrence reimagining the sweeps’ brutalities by disregarding the clear-error standard and claiming that the prolonged and in some cases violent stops were “brief,” and that ICE agents “promptly” let people go. The order precipitated the spread of racialized ICE crackdowns across the country.

We saw it in McMahon v. New York, in which a district court had made concrete findings about the effects on vulnerable students from the administration’s gutting of the Department of Education. The Court, again on the shadow docket, and again along partisan lines, and again ignoring the district court’s factual work, cleared the dismantling—opening a pathway to further mass government firings and to the broader unmaking of the administrative state.

We saw it in Mullin v. Doe, in which a district court had documented Trump’s scurrilous racism toward Haitian immigrants that motivated the cancellation of Temporary Protected Status for 350,000 people. Granting a request from the Trump administration to hear the case early, the Court, along the same ideological lines, rewrote that plain animus out of the record to reinstate deportations.

What is lost when the Court disregards the facts that lower courts have established, and reasons instead from a record of its own, or Trump’s, choosing?

The traditional answer is that a Court that circumvents the messy factual texture of the world and that even declines to go through the motions of the clear-error standard is more likely to get things wrong. America’s constitutional and procedural order gives district courts special fact-finding tools and responsibilities. As a matter of this institutional design and historical custom, American law assumes that district judges are better positioned to find facts.

But there is a deeper reason why a society must care about courts, facts, and clear error: Reckoning with events, people, and actions grounds legal power and protects against the temptations of ideology. Disregarding facts and the procedural conventions that safeguard them does the opposite, risking the substitution of ideology for legal reasoning.

In California, the district court did the work of documenting facts about the world. It probed the evidence and took the world as it found it, unflinching about what the administration is and what it is doing. The highest court in the land ignored this, seeing the world as the justices wished it to be, not as it is.

entries.title: Spencer Cox’s Crusade
entries.summary: The Republican governor thinks he can drain the bile from partisan combat. Trying to do it almost broke him.
entries.content:
The Republican governor thinks he can drain the bile from partisan combat. Trying to do it almost broke him.

On August 9, 2023, Utah’s governor, Spencer Cox, found himself sitting across from Joe Biden in an armored presidential limousine as it idled in downtown Salt Lake City. Working up the nerve to pitch a far-fetched idea, he cleared his throat.

“Mr. President, I know this might sound crazy,” Cox said, “but I think you should pardon Donald Trump.”

Trump was, at the time, facing criminal charges in multiple jurisdictions. He was also the Republican frontrunner for president—a man who had promised to drive “Sleepy Joe” (a.k.a. “Enemy of the State,” a.k.a. “Most Corrupt President We’ve Ever Had,” a.k.a. “Worst President in the History of Our Country”) from the White House and imprison members of the “Biden crime family.”

Cox had no loyalty to Trump; though a Republican, Cox had never voted for him and was hoping that his party would nominate someone else in 2024. But he believed that prosecuting a former president would deepen the country’s political crisis. A pardon by Biden, he argued, could deescalate tensions and interrupt the cycle of partisan retribution.

To Cox’s surprise, Biden perked up at the suggestion. “You know, I’ve actually considered this for a while,” Biden said. “In fact, just this week as we were lying in bed, Jill and I had a long conversation about it.” Biden said that although people were “demanding justice” for Trump, he would seriously consider a pardon.

Cox left the limousine convinced it was a real possibility. Of course, it never happened.

A year later, after a gunman nearly killed Trump at a rally, Cox tried again from the other direction. In a letter to Trump, he wrote, “You have the opportunity to do something that no other person on earth can do right now: unify and save our country.” He offered his support for Trump’s candidacy, and encouraged him to respond to the moment with restraint and magnanimity.

Trump happily accepted the endorsement, which Cox made public at a press conference several days later—but Trump the Great Unifier never materialized. Within days, he was back to railing against “crazy Nancy Pelosi” and riffing on illegal immigrants from insane asylums.

Cox describes his experiences with the two presidents in his new book, Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt, which will be released next month. In the book, these episodes are framed as worthwhile—if ultimately unsuccessful—attempts at depolarization. “When I spoke with President Biden, I hoped he would choose mercy over escalation,” he writes. “When I wrote to President Trump, I hoped he would choose unity over retaliation. In both cases, things didn’t turn out quite the way I’d hoped.”

“It would be fair to suggest I failed,” Cox ventures. Indeed it would. But he prefers not to think of it that way.

Off Ramp is many things—a useful compendium of research on polarization and political violence, a candid memoir of Cox’s uneven attempts at peacemaking, a practical handbook for Americans who want to rediscover how to live with one another. But perhaps more than anything, it is an exercise in an almost-militant optimism that, to skeptics, might border on naivete.

Cox told me that the book had been gestating for more than a decade. He spent years poring over political-science literature and testing his ideas in speeches and interviews; he even launched a project with the National Governors Association: “Disagree Better,” built around the book’s central arguments. But the book acquired a new urgency last year, when Charlie Kirk was assassinated in Utah and Cox was thrust into the international spotlight, where he called on Americans to step back from the brink.

“At some point we have to find an off-ramp,” he said then, “or it’s going to get much, much worse.” When Kirk was murdered, Cox writes, “all of my research became painfully pertinent.”

Throughout the book, and in a series of conversations I’ve had with him recently, Cox seems eager to dispel any notion that he has written another anodyne collection of bromides about bipartisanship and civility. The very word civility—with its connotation of, as he puts it, “a milquetoast politeness that would make Ned Flanders seem aggressive”—makes him cringe. What plagues America right now, in Cox’s telling, is not bad manners, or even political division, but contempt—the conviction that those who don’t share our opinions or values are beneath us and unworthy of good-faith engagement. “Healthy conflict is not a toxic symptom of democracy,” he writes. “It is foundational to it.”

The proposition at the heart of Off Ramp is that political combat can be drained of contempt. As a civic aspiration, it’s hard to argue with. But at this moment? With these leaders? In a system that so strongly rewards reciprocal hatred? Cox knows as well as anyone how difficult it now is to practice the politics he’s preaching.

Last month I visited Cox on his family farm in central Utah, where he led me to the backyard. We sat with his wife, Abby, on wicker furniture overlooking a sprawling pasture with mountains in the distance.

I wanted to ask Cox about a cryptic line in Off Ramp. It appears during the book’s account of the controversy that followed his 2024 endorsement of Trump. Allies and admirers publicly turned on him, he writes; people in his life privately urged him to reconsider. When Cox told one friend that he had prayed about the decision, the friend shot back, “Well, maybe you should pray again.”

None of this surprised me. I had interviewed Cox in the governor’s mansion just a few days after he wrote that letter to Trump, and I remembered how conflicted he seemed even then—how he’d bounced from one rationalization to another, how he’d sounded like he was trying to justify the endorsement to himself as much as to me. I remembered the betrayal expressed by those who’d worked with him in the fight against polarization, as well as the edge in Cox’s voice when he said, “They’re very angry at me, and that’s fine.” The pile-on had clearly been unpleasant.

But what caught my attention was a brief line in the book alluding to what the episode had been like for Cox. “These can be dark and lonely times,” he wrote.

Dark and lonely? I asked Cox to elaborate, and he became quiet.

“I knew there would be backlash,” he told me, tentatively. “It was much stronger than I expected.”

He went on to describe a period of despair and depression that sounded, to my uncertified ear, almost clinical. Close friends and family members condemned his decision and distanced themselves from him. He feared his reputation as a champion of depolarization—developed over years of earnest, painstaking work—was ruined. He spent “a lot of long, dark nights,” he told me, wishing things could go back to how they were.

Cox’s faith, usually a source of comfort in such moments, seemed to make the experience even more fraught. He believes God answers prayers, and he said he’d prayed intensely over whether to endorse. He was quick to clarify that he was not claiming that God wanted Trump to win—but he felt strongly that he was supposed to offer his support to the candidate, for reasons he couldn’t entirely articulate.

As the governor spoke, I noticed that Abby, who had been largely silent throughout our conversation, was pursing her lips. I asked her what she remembered about that summer, and she started to cry.

“In our marriage, I have never seen him like that,” she told me. She was especially hurt that some of the people who criticized Cox most harshly, dismissing him as craven and disingenuous, were those who had the closest relationships with him. “The people who know you best should trust that you aren’t just doing this on a whim.”

I noted that, back in 2024, Abby herself had not been a fan of her husband’s endorsement.

“I’m still not,” she said. “We see things differently. But I trusted him.”

Cox now believes that he was guided to improve his relationship with Trump in 2024 so that he would be prepared to deal with the defining crisis of his governorship a year later: Kirk’s assassination.

During and after the tense 33-hour manhunt for Kirk’s killer, Cox was able to coordinate closely with the Trump administration while also using his high-profile news conferences to offer necessary counterprogramming to the This-means-war rhetoric coming from much of MAGA world. Cox urged calm, condemned all political violence, and called for his fellow Americans to reject politics that “feels like rage.”

This balancing act was widely praised. As my colleague David Graham wrote at the time, “In any other state,” local politicians might have either become targets for Trump “or leapt to inflame the situation. But the Beehive State’s governor is perhaps the most consistent voice of calm and conciliation in the GOP.”

More important, Cox notes, his performance won approval from the president, who largely let the governor lead the official response without interference.

Cox’s critics will no doubt find this narrative self-serving, perhaps even grandiose. But Cox doesn’t seem to care how it looks.

“Charlie’s death could easily have been the match that lit the tinderbox of a nation,” he writes in his book. “However, that didn’t happen, and I hope that at least one small reason for that was the positive relationship that has developed between the president and me. It might have made it easier for him to trust my leadership and allow an off ramp to de-escalation.”

When it came time for Cox to give me a tour of his hometown, he walked me to an old, beat-up pickup truck parked out front and told me to get in. The choice of vehicle was clearly a stunt for my benefit—Cox writes about learning to drive a 1974 Chevy on the farm when he was only 5—but the contrivance didn’t bother me until he casually admitted that this was only the third time he had driven a car since becoming governor five years ago. I buckled my seat belt.

It was the day before Pioneer Day, when Utahns celebrate Brigham Young’s arrival in Salt Lake Valley, and people were already saving their spots on Main Street for the town’s regionally famous parade.

Fairview was settled by Cox’s great-great-great-great grandfather in 1859, and his family is practically built into the infrastructure of the place. He showed me the cemetery where he installed a flagpole for an Eagle Scout project, and the phone company that had been run by the Coxes since 1919, and the various houses he had grown up in.

At my request, we stopped at the Fairview Museum of History and Art, where kitschy pioneer artifacts were arranged in displays with delightfully literal names: the “Tool Room” contained an array of old tools; the “Dentist Room” featured (you guessed it) old dental equipment. An older woman working at the front desk beamed at Cox and remarked how nice it was to see him “all grown-up.”

Cox has deployed Fairview as a device in his speeches for years, and it plays a central role in Off Ramp. He uses his hometown as a stand-in for the qualities America urgently needs: thick community, strong institutions, and the prioritizing of our obligations to one another above the wanton inflammations of politics.

This is hardly an original trope in politicians’ memoirs, but Cox seems to come by his boosterism honestly. He writes that his parents’ divorce, when he was 10, sent him into a spiral of anger, fear, and profound sadness. “Many times,” he writes, “I thought that the world would be a better place without me.” What carried him through was Fairview: the next-door neighbors whose refrigerator was always open to him, the uncle who took him into the mountains and showed him how to herd sheep, the teacher who taught him to love books, the scoutmaster who took him camping. When he felt on the verge of giving up, he writes, they “made my situation their business.”

When Cox became lieutenant governor in 2013, he insisted on keeping his family in Fairview and regularly commuted the roughly 200 miles to Salt Lake City and back—three hours round trip—rather than surrendering his life there. Off Ramp is dedicated “to my family, my friends, and my Fairview.”

Lately, though, Cox has worried that his sanctuary has been breached. The town Facebook group, once a clearinghouse for reports of loose chickens and missing Amazon packages, is periodically littered with comments about Trump and immigration. In the book, Cox describes watching right-wing talk radio transform his father-in-law, a local rancher, from a “beautiful, gracious man” into an angry, combative crank perpetually spoiling for a political fight. (Eventually, a family intervention would pull the man away from talk radio and back to his old self.) Cox himself can relate to the deleterious effects of excessive political-news consumption: In one admirably unflattering passage, he writes about his own addiction to Twitter and its “information heroin.” It got so bad that he had to delete social-media apps from his phone.

Cox seems to recognize the dangers of publishing a book like this. No matter how many self-effacing caveats he includes, he risks looking like he’s holding himself up as a role model of civic virtue. The truth, he says, is that the precepts he articulates don’t come naturally to him.

“I’m a hothead,” he told me. “I’ve gotten punched in the face. I’ve punched people in the face.” Once he was even kicked out of a game while coaching his kid’s flag-football game. “That’s who I am.”

He said he works to temper those impulses, which seem omnipresent in our politics, but that he doesn’t always succeed. “It’s hard to be the Disagree Better guy, because you’re under a microscope,” Cox said. “When I say something disrespectful or lash out, people pounce.”

In Off Ramp, he revisits a moment at a Utah Republican convention, when, after being booed by Trump supporters, he snapped: “Maybe you hate that I don’t hate enough.” The retort was so satisfying in the moment. “The words coming out of my mouth felt good,” he writes. But he later came to regret it—he had answered contempt with contempt, making it that much harder for him and his opponents to understand one another. In the weeks afterward, he personally apologized to some of the people who had booed him.

A similar episode took place at a Disagree Better event at George Washington University, when a student confronted him over Utah’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors, linking it to suicide rates among transgender kids. Cox responded defensively, accusing the student of “bad faith.” “I want these kids to thrive,” he said. “I want these kids to be successful.” But, he continued, “I think there’s a better way to do that than having genital-mutilation surgeries before they’re 18." Cox, quickly catching himself, said he should have given his interlocutor the last word, and invited the student backstage after the event to keep talking.

But even as Cox tries to model healthy political debate, he rejects the idea—often floated by his critics—that “disagreeing better” means never staking out controversial positions or supporting divisive policies. “I’m going to be a partisan,” he told me. “I want my team to win. When my team wins, we’re going to try to implement those things.” Politics, he told me, doesn’t have to rid itself of partisanship to become less contemptuous.

When I asked Cox whether he ever worries that his optimism is misplaced, he answered immediately: “I think about that every day.” He does not pretend, he told me, that “a book from a governor of Utah is going to change the course of history.”

But he remains stubbornly hopeful that America’s political culture is ready for a reset. He cites letters from people who have reconciled with their parents after politics had poisoned their relationships, and Disagree Better workshops attended by hundreds of legislators and policy makers. He’s convinced that the movement is growing, though he concedes that the evidence is mostly anecdotal.

“We’ll have an actual measuring stick soon,” he told me, “when we see if people buy the book.”
